strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck in GUI agents: accurate visual grounding on high-resolution, cluttered interfaces. Reframing grounding as cursor-mediated interaction is intuitive, useful, and well motivated by the limitations of one-shot coordinate generation.

The empirical gains are meaningful. GUI-CURSOR reports state-of-the-art average accuracy on ScreenSpot-v2 (93.9%) and especially ScreenSpot-Pro (56.5%), with a large improvement over prior RL-based grounding methods on the harder high-resolution benchmark.

The method is reasonably concrete: the paper specifies the interactive environment, STOP/move actions, GRPO objective, dense position reward, trajectory penalties, and cursor-centric focusing strategy. The ablations indicate that trajectory penalties, thinking tokens, and CCF each contribute to performance.

The analysis sections add useful insight beyond headline numbers, including zero-shot cursor-moving tests, movement-step statistics, training dynamics, and a synthetic cursor-in-box probe suggesting improved spatial reasoning after training.
The writing is mostly clear, and the figures/case studies make the proposed interaction loop easy to understand.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully isolate the claimed benefit of multi-step interactive refinement. After CCF, only 0.5% of ScreenSpot-v2 and 9.4% of ScreenSpot-Pro examples use more than one movement step, so much of the gain may come from better one-step grounding, training regularization, or crop-based inference rather than genuine iterative search.

The comparison to baselines is somewhat difficult to interpret. The method uses Qwen2.5-VL-7B, RL training, and CCF, while many baselines differ in backbone, training resolution, data, and inference procedure. The paper does apply a focus strategy to GTA1/GUI-G2, which helps, but a stronger controlled comparison with identical backbone, data, resolution, and RL budget would make the central claim more convincing.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as exact training data size, sampling proportions from Aria-UI and OS-Atlas, filtering scripts, validation split, random seeds, compute time, and full hyperparameter search are not sufficiently specified. The manuscript also does not clearly commit to releasing code, prompts, checkpoints, or evaluation scripts.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates. Reported improvements, especially the smaller ScreenSpot-v2 gains, are not accompanied by confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests, despite RL training and online filtering potentially introducing variance.

Some reward and objective details are underspecified or potentially fragile. The position reward definition is ambiguous outside the box after distance normalization, penalty weights appear empirically chosen, and the GRPO objective/equation presentation has notation issues that could hinder independent implementation.

The method has practical limitations that are acknowledged only partly: CCF can miss targets when the initial prediction is far away, with 10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro examples reportedly outside the focused area; the iterative setup increases inference cost; and negative examples show the model may hallucinate multi-action procedures despite the task being single-point grounding.

The cursor-in-box probe is interesting but preliminary. It uses synthetic white-background images and reports heatmaps without aggregate metrics or comparisons to more models, so it only weakly supports broad claims about improved general spatial reasoning.
The paper has minor presentation issues, including cramped tables, typographical errors, and some overstrong language around spatial understanding given the limited causal evidence.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and intuitive reframing of GUI grounding as an interactive cursor-search problem, with visual feedback after each predicted coordinate. This is a useful perspective for a task where direct coordinate generation is known to be brittle.
The reported benchmark numbers are strong: 93.9% on ScreenSpot-v2 and 56.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, with particularly large gains on the harder high-resolution ScreenSpot-Pro setting.

The paper includes meaningful ablations over trajectory penalties, explicit reasoning tokens, and cursor-centric focusing, plus diagnostic analyses such as movement-step statistics, training dynamics, and a cursor-in-box spatial reasoning probe.

The limitations around cursor-centric focusing are at least partly acknowledged, including that the crop can miss the target when the initial prediction is poor, affecting 10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro examples.
weaknesses: The central claim that multi-step interactive visual feedback is the main driver is not convincingly established. After CCF, the model takes more than one step on only 0.5% of ScreenSpot-v2 and 9.4% of ScreenSpot-Pro examples, so most reported gains appear to come from one-step prediction plus cropping rather than iterative search.

The strongest ScreenSpot-Pro gain is heavily dependent on cursor-centric focusing: performance drops from 56.5% to 45.3% without CCF, below GTA1's reported 50.1%. Although the authors apply a similar focus trick to GTA1 and GUI-G2, the comparison still does not isolate whether the proposed RL cursor training is necessary versus a stronger same-resolution, same-data one-step baseline with the same crop/focus inference.

The experimental protocol leaves fairness questions unresolved. Many baselines appear to be taken from the literature with different training data, resolutions, inference budgets, and possibly different test-time strategies; no controlled reimplementation of the most relevant baselines under the same data and compute budget is provided.

The adaptive multi-step behavior is overstated. The claim that the model adaptively conducts more steps on difficult examples is supported mainly by correlations with target size and a small fraction of multi-step cases, not by causal evidence that additional steps substantially improve final accuracy across many examples.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives some hyperparameters, GPU count, and prompts, but lacks exact training set size, sampling details, preprocessing/filtering specifics, random seeds, variance over runs, wall-clock/training cost, and a clear code/model release plan. This is problematic for an RL method with online filtering and stochastic trajectory sampling.

Several analyses are suggestive but under-specified. The cursor-in-box probe reports heatmaps but not dataset size, exact box/cursor distributions, aggregate scores, or statistical uncertainty. The thinking-token ablation is also hard to interpret because it changes both output format and reasoning supervision/inference behavior.

Presentation quality is uneven. Tables have formatting/extraction issues, some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants, and there are grammar and notation problems. These do not alone determine the score, but they make the technical story less precise.

The paper does not discuss broader risks of GUI agents in any depth, such as unsafe automated actions, privacy exposure in screenshots, or deployment safeguards. The work is mostly benchmark-oriented, but this omission is still relevant for GUI-control systems.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful reframing of GUI grounding as an interactive cursor-search problem with visual feedback, rather than only one-shot coordinate prediction. This is a meaningful idea for high-resolution GUI settings where coordinate-token alignment is brittle.

The empirical results are strong on the target benchmarks: GUI-CURSOR reports 93.9% on ScreenSpot-v2 and 56.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, with a particularly large improvement on the harder ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark over prior 7B-scale methods.

The ablations are substantive. The paper separately studies trajectory penalties, explicit thinking, cursor-centric focusing, movement-step behavior, and zero-shot cursor movement, which helps support the claim that the interaction formulation and reward design matter.
The analysis of movement behavior is helpful: the model uses additional steps more often on ScreenSpot-Pro and on smaller targets, which is consistent with the intended adaptive refinement story.
The cursor-in-box diagnostic is a nice addition. It gives some evidence that the training procedure improves cursor-relative spatial reasoning beyond benchmark-specific coordinate prediction.
The presentation is generally clear, with a well-motivated problem statement, readable method description, detailed appendices, and useful qualitative examples including failure cases.
weaknesses: A substantial part of the headline gain appears to come from cursor-centric focusing rather than the multi-step interaction itself. Without CCF, GUI-CURSOR is below GTA1 on ScreenSpot-Pro, and applying a similar focus strategy to GTA1 narrows the gap to 56.5 vs. 54.0. This does not invalidate the contribution, but it makes the central causal story less clean.

The learned policy usually performs only one post-focus movement: more-than-one-step movement occurs in only 0.5% of ScreenSpot-v2 and 9.4% of ScreenSpot-Pro examples. This weakens the claim that multi-step refinement is broadly responsible for the improvements.

The evaluation is limited to GUI grounding benchmarks. There is no end-to-end GUI-agent evaluation showing that higher point accuracy translates into more reliable task completion or safer interaction in real applications.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper gives many hyperparameters and implementation details, but it does not clearly specify exact training set sizes, sampled data composition, filtering outcomes, random seeds, variance across runs, or whether code/model checkpoints will be released.

The comparison fairness is somewhat mixed because baselines differ in training resolution and inference-time strategies. The authors partially address this by adding focus to GTA1 and GUI-G2, but a more systematic equal-compute/equal-resolution comparison would strengthen the evidence.
The paper lacks uncertainty estimates or significance testing, which matters because some differences on ScreenSpot-v2 are small and the method involves stochastic RL training.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The CCF failure mode is honestly discussed, but broader risks of GUI agents, erroneous clicks, automation misuse, and safeguards for real-world deployment are not treated in depth.
Some minor presentation issues remain, including typos and notation problems such as the GRPO advantage equation formatting, but these do not substantially impede understanding.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and important problem in GUI agents: precise grounding on high-resolution, visually complex interfaces where direct coordinate prediction is brittle.

The core idea of reframing GUI grounding as an interactive cursor-search process with visual feedback is intuitive, well motivated, and practically relevant. The reward design targets plausible failure modes such as false stopping, moving away from the target, and repeated coordinates.

The empirical results are broad and generally strong. GUI-CURSOR improves over strong supervised and RL baselines on ScreenSpot-Pro, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, ScreenSpot-v2, and OSWorld agentic evaluation, including comparisons using the same base model family.

The paper includes useful ablations for trajectory penalties, thinking tokens, cursor-centric focusing, movement step budgets, and training dynamics. These analyses make the behavior of the method more interpretable than a simple leaderboard-style result.

The appendices provide meaningful implementation detail, including GRPO objective, rollout procedure, hyperparameters, prompts, latency/throughput measurements, and qualitative positive and negative examples.
The limitations discussion is more candid than usual. The authors explicitly discuss out-of-crop failures, cursor occlusion, click-only scope, latency, and extensions to continuous interactions.
weaknesses: A large fraction of the reported gain appears tied to cursor-centric focusing rather than the interactive cursor-moving formulation itself. On ScreenSpot-Pro, GUI-CURSOR without CCF is reported below GTA1, while CCF also improves GTA1. This weakens the central claim that visual feedback and multi-step cursor movement are the decisive cause of the gains.

The multi-step interaction aspect is less prominent in practice than the framing suggests. The model uses more than one post-CCF movement on only 9.4% of ScreenSpot-Pro examples and 0.5% of ScreenSpot-v2 examples, and two-step inference captures nearly all of the full max-4 performance. This makes the contribution closer to a strong two-stage refinement/cropping system than a general interactive search method.

The comparison to baselines is extensive but not perfectly controlled. Different methods use different training resolutions, sample counts, base models, and sometimes extra focusing or verifier mechanisms. The paper partially addresses this, but the causal attribution among RL, CCF, cursor rendering, prompts, and base-model priors remains somewhat entangled.

The method depends on an initial coarse prediction; the authors report that about 10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro cases crop out the target, and the proposed zero-shot target-presence detector is unreliable. This is a material failure mode for high-resolution or cluttered settings.

The spatial reasoning probes are interesting but limited. The cursor-in-box synthetic test is very different from real GUI grounding, and improvements on it do not by themselves establish robust spatial understanding. The broader spatial benchmark gains are modest and sometimes mixed.

Reproducibility is acceptable but not complete. The manuscript gives many details, but reliable reproduction would still require released code, exact training/evaluation splits, preprocessing/filtering scripts, model checkpoints, cursor rendering implementation, and full prompts/configs for all baselines.

The writing is mostly clear, but some claims are overstated. Statements that the method learns better spatial reasoning from visual feedback should be softened or more carefully separated from improvements due to CCF and task-specific RL optimization.

Ethical discussion is minimal. GUI agents can execute destructive or privacy-sensitive actions, and more discussion is needed on safe deployment, user confirmation, failure recovery, and risks from hallucinated action sequences such as those shown in the negative examples.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful reframing of GUI grounding as cursor-based iterative search, with a concrete training environment, trajectory rewards, and an inference-time crop/focus mechanism. The idea is intuitive and relevant for high-resolution GUI grounding.

The empirical scope is broad: ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, OSWorld agentic evaluation, and additional spatial reasoning probes. The strongest reported numbers on ScreenSpot-Pro and UI-Vision are meaningful, especially for icon/small-target cases.

The appendix contains helpful implementation details, latency measurements, training dynamics, ablations of trajectory penalties, and an honest discussion of out-of-crop failures and cursor occlusion.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not well isolated. Much of the gain appears to come from cursor-centric focusing/cropping rather than iterative cursor reasoning: GUI-CURSOR without CCF is below GTA1 on ScreenSpot-Pro, while adding a similar focus step to GTA1 closes much of the gap. After CCF, only 9.4% of ScreenSpot-Pro and 0.5% of ScreenSpot-v2 examples use more than one movement, so the method is often effectively a two-stage crop-and-predict system rather than an adaptive multi-step search.

Comparisons are not fully controlled. Baselines use different resolutions, training data amounts, base models, and inference-time focusing/verifier strategies. The paper acknowledges GUI-CURSOR uses lower training resolution than GTA1, but then makes strong claims about the cursor-learning paradigm from results that conflate training resolution, CCF, RL recipe, prompting/thinking, and backbone choice.

The OSWorld online evaluation is under-supported: it uses an o3 planner, reports very few settings, compares different step budgets against prior results, and gives no variance or repeated trials. This makes the agentic performance claim weaker than the headline suggests.

The spatial reasoning evidence is suggestive but not decisive. The cursor-in-box task is synthetic and close to the training intervention; improvements on SPHERE/SpatialMQA are modest, and the paper does not rule out generic RL/fine-tuning effects or prompt-format effects. The claim that GUI-CURSOR obtains broadly better out-of-distribution spatial reasoning is therefore overstated.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript provides hyperparameters, but not exact sampled training examples, seeds, full preprocessing details, code/model release commitments, or enough detail to reproduce all baseline adaptations such as CCF-on-GTA1/GUI-G2 and RegionFocus comparisons. Several results rely on newly cited 2025/2026 baselines and external proprietary models, further limiting independent verification.

Presentation has notable issues: some tables/claims are inconsistent or confusing, e.g. Table 11 labels a Qwen2.5 GUI-CURSOR row with the UI-TARS ScreenSpot-Pro/OSWorld-G numbers, and the GRPO objective/advantage equations appear typographically malformed. These issues do not invalidate the whole paper but reduce confidence.

The impact statement is boilerplate and inadequate for GUI agents. A method that improves GUI automation can affect privacy, account misuse, security-sensitive actions, and accessibility workflows; the manuscript should discuss safeguards and misuse risks rather than state that no societal consequences need highlighting.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful reframing of GUI grounding as an interactive cursor-search problem rather than one-shot coordinate prediction. The idea is simple, well motivated by the visual feedback gap in existing coordinate-generation approaches, and plausibly useful for GUI agents.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall: results cover ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, OSWorld agentic evaluation, spatial-reasoning probes, and comparisons to both SFT and RL grounding baselines. The gains on the difficult ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark and the OSWorld agentic setting are especially meaningful.

The ablations are a strong part of the paper. The authors isolate trajectory penalties, thinking tokens, cursor-centric focusing, movement-step budgets, and training dynamics, which makes the contribution more interpretable than a pure benchmark-improvement paper.

The method appears relatively data-efficient: the manuscript reports stronger ScreenSpot-Pro performance with 8K samples than baselines using substantially more data, and includes useful training/inference efficiency analysis.

The appendices provide many implementation details, including the GRPO objective, rollout procedure, hyperparameters, cursor size, training resolution, decoding settings, prompts, latency, and qualitative examples. This supports reproducibility, though not completely.
The paper is mostly well written and the main conceptual distinction from iterative cropping/test-time scaling methods is explained clearly.
weaknesses: The central claim that GUI-CURSOR improves general spatial reasoning is suggestive but not fully established. The cursor-in-box probe is useful, and SpatialMQA/SPHERE gains are positive, but the improvements are modest on some categories and could be partly due to RL adaptation, prompting format, or GUI-domain training rather than the cursor mechanism specifically. More controlled comparisons against non-cursor multi-step RL or matched visual-feedback variants would strengthen this claim.

The strongest benchmark results depend substantially on cursor-centric focusing. The paper acknowledges that without CCF, GUI-CURSOR can underperform GTA1 on ScreenSpot-Pro, which means the performance gain is partly due to an inference-time cropping strategy rather than only the learned cursor-feedback policy.

The online OSWorld evaluation is promising but somewhat thin: only headline success rates are shown, apparently without confidence intervals, multiple seeds, task breakdowns, or variance over runs. Given the stochasticity and cost of online GUI-agent evaluation, uncertainty estimates would be important.

Reproducibility is adequate but incomplete. The paper gives many training details, but I did not see a clear commitment to release code, trained checkpoints, preprocessing scripts, exact sampled training split, or evaluation harnesses. Some comparisons also appear to mix reported baseline numbers and reimplemented variants, which can make exact reproduction difficult.

The impact/ethics statement is very cursory. Since GUI agents can automate user interfaces and potentially perform unintended or harmful actions, the paper should discuss risks such as unsafe automation, permission boundaries, privacy exposure from screenshots, and robustness failures in real GUI environments.

Presentation has some polish issues: there are repeated spacing/formatting artifacts in model names and tables, occasional typos, and some tables are dense enough that readability suffers. These do not undermine the technical contribution, but they should be cleaned up.
